sentences.text: This bipedal predator possessed dozens of large, sharp teeth in its jaws alongside small, two-fingered forelimbs.
Adult individuals measured between 8 and 9 meters in length and weighed between 2 and 3 metric tons.
The longest known skull measures 99 centimeters, which is slightly smaller than that of the related Daspletosaurus.
At the front of the snout, eight premaxillary teeth were smaller than the others, closely spaced, and D-shaped in cross-section.
More than twenty complete skeletons have been discovered, making it one of the best-represented tyrannosaurids in the fossil record.
A 2023 report described a juvenile Gorgosaurus fossil containing the intact remains of two juvenile Citipes in its stomach.
The presence of only hindlimb and tail vertebrae in the stomach suggests juvenile Gorgosaurus preferentially consumed the muscular hindlimbs of its prey.
A Saurornitholestes jawbone found in the Dinosaur Park Formation bears tooth marks from a bite by a young tyrannosaur, possibly Gorgosaurus.
The genus Gorgosaurus was named by Lambe in 1914, and the holotype specimen NMC 2120 was discovered in 1913 by Charles M. Sternberg.
Charles Whitney Gilmore named a small tyrannosaurid skull from Montana Gorgosaurus lancensis in 1946.
As an apex predator, Gorgosaurus preyed on abundant ceratopsids and hadrosaurs.
Researchers estimate that Gorgosaurus underwent a dietary shift when its lower jaw reached a length of 58 cm.
Gorgosaurus spent up to half of its life in a juvenile phase before reaching near-maximum size in just a few years.
The holotype of Gorgosaurus libratus shows healed fractures on the 13th and 14th gastralia, the left fibula, and the third right dorsal rib.
Another specimen bears a 10 cm longitudinal fracture in the middle of its right fibula.
In 1970, Dale Russell hypothesized that Gorgosaurus hunted fleet-footed hadrosaurs while Daspletosaurus hunted ceratopsians and ankylosaurians.
Evidence from Montana suggests Daspletosaurus also ate hadrosaurs, challenging the idea that it only hunted armored dinosaurs.
The main debate in Gorgosaurus paleobiology concerns whether it was a scavenger or a hunter, based on anatomical comparisons with coexisting tyrannosaurid species and ecological niche parameters.
Gorgosaurus is classified in the family Tyrannosauridae.
Gorgosaurus belongs to the parent group Albertosaurinae.
Gorgosaurus is sometimes considered a junior synonym of Albertosaurus because Albertosaurus was named first.
Gorgosaurus and Albertosaurus are extremely similar, with distinctions found mainly in subtle differences in their teeth and skull bones.
Gorgosaurus lived in western North America during the Late Cretaceous Period (Campanian) between approximately 76.5 and 73 million years ago.
Gorgosaurus libratus fossils from the Dinosaur Park Formation date to between 76.6 and 75.1 million years ago during the middle Campanian stage.
Gorgosaurus lived in North America between 76.5 and 75.1 million years ago during the late Cretaceous period.
Fossils were found in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada.
Gorgosaurus inhabited a lush floodplain environment located along the edge of an inland sea.
Some experts debate whether Gorgosaurus libratus is a distinct species or merely a synonym of the genus Albertosaurus.
It is debated whether Gorgosaurus and Albertosaurus should be maintained as separate genera or combined into one.
Some experts consider G. libratus to be a species of the genus Albertosaurus due to the extreme similarity between the two genera.
